items.rule: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal.
items.example: \text{If one corresponding angle is }65^\circ,\text{ the other is }65^\circ

items.rule: When a transversal cuts parallel lines, alternate interior angles are equal.
items.example: \text{If an alternate interior angle is }72^\circ,\text{ its pair is }72^\circ

items.rule: Interior angles on the same side of a transversal are supplementary.
The three interior angles of every triangle sum to 180 degrees.
An exterior angle equals the sum of the two non-adjacent interior angles.
When two lines intersect, vertically opposite angles are equal.
Adjacent angles whose non-common arms form a straight line are supplementary.

concepts.title: 1. Corresponding, Alternate & Co-interior Angles
concepts.subtitle: Reading Relationships Across Parallel Lines
concepts.summary: A transversal crossing two parallel lines creates predictable angle relationships. Corresponding and alternate interior angles are equal, while co-interior angles are supplementary.

points.text: Corresponding: Angles in matching positions at the two intersections are equal when the lines are parallel.
Alternate Interior: Interior angles on opposite sides of the transversal are equal.
Co-interior: Interior angles on the same side of the transversal add to $180^\circ$.
Memory Cue: Corresponding = same position, Alternate = opposite sides inside, Co-interior = same side inside.

concepts.formula: l_1\parallel l_2\implies\text{Corresponding angles equal, Alternate interior angles equal, Co-interior angles sum to }180^\circ
concepts.trap: Do not treat every pair of angles formed by parallel lines as equal. First identify whether the pair is corresponding, alternate interior, or co-interior.

concepts.title: 2. Angle-Sum in a Triangle
concepts.subtitle: The 180° Triangle Rule
concepts.summary: Every triangle has exactly 180 degrees across its three interior angles. Use this invariant to find missing angles after identifying the known ones.

points.text: Interior Sum: The three interior angles always add to $180^\circ$.
Unknown Angle: Subtract the sum of the known angles from $180^\circ$.
Angle Chase: Combine the triangle rule with parallel-line or vertically opposite relationships when needed.

concepts.trap: Do not apply the 180° rule to exterior angles as though they were all interior. Identify the angle location first.

concepts.title: 3. Exterior Angle Theorem
concepts.subtitle: Connecting Outside and Inside Angles
concepts.summary: An exterior angle of a triangle equals the sum of the two interior angles opposite it. It can also be viewed through the linear-pair relationship.

points.text: Exterior Angle: Extend one side of a triangle to create an angle outside the triangle.
Remote Interior Angles: The two interior angles not adjacent to the exterior angle are added.
Equivalent Check: Exterior angle and its adjacent interior angle form a linear pair and sum to $180^\circ$.

concepts.trap: Do not add the exterior angle's adjacent interior angle to the two remote interior angles. The theorem uses only the two non-adjacent interior angles.

concepts.title: 4. Vertically Opposite Angles
concepts.subtitle: Intersecting-Line Symmetry
concepts.summary: When two straight lines intersect, the opposite angles form equal pairs. Adjacent angles form linear pairs and sum to 180 degrees.

points.text: Vertically Opposite: Opposite angles at an intersection are equal.
Linear Pair: Adjacent angles along a straight line sum to $180^\circ$.
Angle Chase: Find one angle, use vertical equality for its opposite, then use supplementary relationships for adjacent angles.

concepts.trap: Only opposite angles are automatically equal. Adjacent angles at an intersection are generally supplementary, not equal.
